newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan says Fed to act if growth doesn't slow.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan says Fed to act if growth doesn't slow.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Thursday he expects economic growth to slow later this year and into next, but added that the central bank would need to act if that does not prove to be the case.
In a speech for delivery to New York University's Stern School of Business, Greenspan said the Fed has to be wary because the economy seems to have little slack now.
"Should the expected slowing in the growth of demand fail to materialize, we would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets," the Fed chief said.

The central bank in March raised short-term interest rates for the first time in more than two years in an effort to keep the economy from overheating and thus sustain the expansion. It holds its next policy-making meeting on May 20.
Greenspan spent much of his speech defending the Fed's quarter percentage point rate increase on March 25 against what he called "more than the usual share of ... criticism."
"The (central bank's) Federal Open Market Committee raised rates as a form of insurance," Greenspan said. "It was a small, prudent step."

He argued that a modest tightening of Fed policy to guard against the risk of excessive credit made sense even if in retrospect the move turned out to be unnecessary because its effect on the economy would be small and temporary.

"I viewed our small (rate) increase...as taken not so much as a consequence of a change in the most probable forecast of moderate growth and low inflation later this year and next, but rather to address the probability that being wrong had materially increased," Greenspan said.
Lawmakers from both major political parties, businessmen and labor unions all criticized the central bank for raising rates at a time when inflation has remained low.

Greenspan acknowledged that there was scant evidence of any imminent resurgence of inflation now. But he argued that the Fed cannot wait for clearly visible signs of emerging inflation before acting because then it would be behind the curve in the fight to contain price pressures.
"To be sure, 1997 is not 1994 when the Fed was forced to tighten monetary conditions very substantially to avoid accomodating rising inflation," Greenspan said.

He said that pressures in product markets -- markets for goods -- have remained tame, with companies running their factories and other operations at levels a little below those that prevailed through much of 1994.

"To be sure, since early 1995, those pressures have eased off," Greenspan said. "However, falling unemployment rates and rising overtime hours -- as well as anecdotal reports -- unambiguously point to growing tightness in labor markets."

The unemployment rate tumbled last month to 4.9 percent, its lowest level in 23 years. The overall economy grew at 5.6 percent annualized clip in the first quarter, its fastest pace in more than nine years.

With labor markets tight and little slack in product markets, Greenspan said that persistently strong economic growth above its long-term trend would lead to higher long-term interest rates in financial markets. If the Fed tries to accomodate the excess demand by keeping short-term rates down, it would end up hurting the economy.
Greenspan was upbeat about the economy's longer-term outlook. "Looking ahead, there are many reasons to be optimistic about the economy's prospects," he said.

But he said that the United States could take a number of steps to make the outlook even better. Keeping inflation low was one. Reining in government outlays on entitlement programs such as Medicare health benefits for the elderly another.
Lower taxes on income and capital gains, deregulation and a balanced federal budget also would also help promote long-term economic growth, he said.
